gpcs.notes: Open-syllable a says its name (long a) before a single consonant + vowel, e.g. na-vy, a-pron.
AU/UK BATH-set words (bath, grass, dance, last) take /ar/ here; US speakers say /a/ in the same words — accent-specific.
w before a changes its sound from /a/ to /o/: want, wash, swan, wander.
Unstressed a reduces to schwa in the weak syllable.
Soft c: c says /s/ only before e, i or y.
Open-syllable e says its name (long e) before a single consonant + vowel.
Soft g: g says /j/ before e, i or y (with many exceptions e.g. get, give).
Open-syllable i says its name (long i) before a single consonant + vowel: ti-ger, si-lent.
k spells /k/ before e, i, y (kit, key) and at the end of a word after a consonant or long vowel (ink, oak).
Open-syllable o says its name (long o) before a single consonant + vowel: o-pen, go.
A handful of very common words spell short /u/ with o.
q is always followed by u in English; together they spell /kw/.
Word-final/medial s often says /z/; this is also how the plural -s sounds after a voiced sound (dogs, runs).
Open-syllable u often says its 'name', /yoo/.
English words don't end in i, so final /igh/ at the end of a (usually 1-syllable) word is spelled y.
y stands in for short i mid-word, mostly in words of Greek origin.
Unstressed final y at the end of a longer word says /ee/.
au never ends a word — that job belongs to aw.
ay is the go-to spelling of /ay/ at the end of a word/syllable.
Greek-origin ch says /k/ (school, chemist, chaos).
French-origin ch says /sh/.
ck is used straight after a short vowel at the end of a word/syllable (neck, not neek).
dge is used straight after a short vowel; ge is used after a consonant or long vowel/team.
-ed says /d/ after a voiced sound.
-ed says /t/ after an unvoiced sound.
-ed adds a whole extra syllable, /id/, after a base word already ending in /t/ or /d/.
'i before e except after c' — after c, ei says /ee/.
Realisation varies — 'either' has both /igh/ and /ee/ pronunciations across accents.
Unstressed word-final -er is schwa in AU/UK, r-coloured in US.
Yod-dropping: many US speakers say plain /oo_long/ after n/t/d/l/s.
Non-standard/dialectal realisation of unstressed final -ey; most accents say /ee/ (see ey.ee) — kept only for this one classic teaching example.
Silent u after g keeps g hard before e/i.
y at the end of a base word changes to ie before -s (y-to-i rule).
Unstressed -ous ending reduces to schwa, not a full STRUT vowel.
Same spelling as unvoiced th.th — voicing is contrastive but unmarked in print.
wh says plain /w/ for AU/UK and most US speakers; the historic /hw/ contrast survives only in some accents.
w before or changes its sound from /or/ to /er/.
Magic/split e: a says its name, the e is silent.
Least common split digraph — many /ee/ words prefer ee/ea instead.
tch is used straight after a short vowel (match); plain ch elsewhere (much, bench, lunch, teach).
English words don't end in bare v — add a silent e.
Silent e keeps c soft (/s/) at the end of a word.
Silent e keeps g soft (/j/) at the end of a word.
b is silent after m at the end of a word.
Adds a new syllable /iz/ when the base word already ends in a hissing/buzzing sound (s, ss, x, z, ch, sh).
There/where are heart-word exceptions where ere says /air/, not /ear/.
w before ar changes its sound from /ar/ to /or/.
l is silent; al says /or/ before k.
Exceptions with short o: cost, lost, frost.
Final stable syllable: le is unstressed and the e is silent; the l is often syllabic. Often taught as 'le says /el/'.
Unstressed word-final -or reduces to schwa, same sound as -er/-a in teacher/sofa.
Unstressed o reduces to schwa in a weak syllable.
The most common spelling of the NEAR vowel (contrast eer.ear: deer, cheer).
Rare and unstable — many speakers merge this with /or/ (see phonemes.json note on 'ure').
UFLI-style 'glued sound' — short a blends tightly with a following m; taught as one chunk for fluency, same phonemes as a.a + m.m.
UFLI-style 'glued sound' — short a blends tightly with a following n; same phonemes as a.a + n.n.
Glued sound: vowel quality shifts slightly before ng.
Glued sound (as a rime, e.g. king/sing) — the same spelling also carries the verb suffix -ing (jumping, running).
Glued sound: vowel quality shifts slightly before ng.
Glued sound: vowel quality shifts slightly before ng.
Glued sound: n before k is pronounced /ng/ (velar nasal), not /n/.
Glued sound: n before k is pronounced /ng/ (velar nasal), not /n/.
Glued sound: n before k is pronounced /ng/ (velar nasal), not /n/.
Glued sound: n before k is pronounced /ng/ (velar nasal), not /n/.
Superlative suffix -est.
